newsitem.title: USA: Ford European results to get close scrutiny.
newsitem.headline: Ford European results to get close scrutiny.

text.p: When Ford Motor Co. releases its fourth quarter earnings Wednesday all eyes will be glued to the performance of its European operations, which, industry analysts said Monday, they expect to again show deep losses.
Ford, like all automakers in Europe, is struggling to hold its own in a market where the popularity of small, low-profit cars, a bruising price war and new competitors have cut margins to the bone.

As Ford wrestles to bring its European cost structure in line with the market realities, the company's recent troubles have turned a harsh spotlight on its much-vaunted Ford 2000 reorganization -- and caused some investors to question the viability of the project, analysts said.
Wertheim Schroder analyst John Casesa said the steep losses in Europe should be interpreted as more evidence Ford needs to accelerate its global product development restructuring.
"I think Ford 2000 is the medicine, but I think we were all surprised at how sick the patient is," Casesa said.

In its most dramatic action since posting a $472 million European third quarter loss, Ford said Jan. 16 it will cut 1,300 of the 4,500 jobs at its Halewood, England, plant -- one of three that makes the Escort in Europe.

Analysts predict the fourth quarter European loss will be smaller, although it could still be more than $300 million. Ford Chairman Alex Trotman has said he expects the European operations to be profitable for all of 1997. Ford of Europe lost $203 million through the first nine months of 1996 vs. a $164 million profit for the same 1995 period.
Nicholas Lobaccaro, an analyst at Bear Stearns, said over the long term, Ford will have to take more severe steps.
"Ultimately, to become structurally profitable it's going to take some plant closings and realignment of their production base," he said.

Burnham Securities Inc. analyst David Healy said he believed Ford has problems in Europe for two reasons: it produces too many of its vehicles in high-cost Germany; and it doesn't have a high-profit margin vehicle.
Indeed, analysts agreed that Ford desperately needed a high-end product with fat margins.

In the United States, full-size pickup trucks and sport utility vehicles have kept the company's vehicle operations afloat. But in Europe, much of Ford's sales strength is concentrated in low-profit small cars such as the new Ka and Fiesta.

Sales of Ford's European top-end car, the Scorpio, have sputtered badly as consumers were turned off by its controversial redesign two years ago. The last two Escorts also have been big disappointments, leaving Ford hobbled in Europe's biggest market segment.
The automaker also is pressing ahead with the Ford 2000 initiative, even as more signs surface the system is not working as planned.

Launched at the beginning of 1995, the plan combined Ford's traditionally separate North American and European product development organisations and set up five vehicle centres -- four in the Detroit area and one in Europe. Some industry executives say Ford's European engineering base -- split between Cologne, Germany and Dunton, England -- is a source of unnecessary duplication for the automaker.
Rather than developing cars and trucks in the markets where they would be sold, Ford 2000 is aiming for "world" vehicles that could be tailored for individual markets.
Earlier this month, published reports said prototypes of the next-generation Escort, designed in Europe, were a hit with European buyers, but U.S. consumer focus groups panned the styling.
Last October, the company cut the number of vehicle centres back to three, saying it has been able to streamline its organisational structure more than originally thought.

Speaking to reporters earlier this month, Ford's Trotman said the company was more committed than ever to Ford 2000, which was launched at his direction. So far, the company has been able to slash $11 billion from what it expects to spend on global product development programmes from 1996-2000.
